docs.title: Soul Factory
docs.text:
Launch, manage, and govern AI agents — without building the infrastructure.

Soul Factory is a native DataRobot app that gives every person in your org a front door to the dr-claw agent runtime. Business users get a one-click agent catalog. Developers get a forkable runtime. Admins get full fleet governance.

Get started → Core Concepts App Flow

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Concept Description Soul The agent's identity — a SOUL.md the runtime reads on every request, hot-swappable with zero downtime Pack Role-based agent template — pre-configured soul + tools for a specific job Domain Active soul loaded via souls/.active — set per-agent, switchable live Session A running agent instance — chat history, SSE log stream, tool calls, HITL events HITL Human-in-the-loop gate — write operations held for admin approval before execution OpenShell Envoy-based tool firewall — every MCP call is allowed, blocked, or queued and logged

Full definitions →

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Browse packs — pick a domain pack (core, data, dev, mlops). Each surfaces a pre-configured soul + tool set.

2. Configure — Name your agent, set HITL rules, pick allowed models. Four fields. Under 2 minutes.

3. Launch — Soul Factory creates the DR Workload, wires LLM Gateway and Global MCP, runs a health check. Live.

4. Interact — Chat via Web UI. The agent executes MCP tools, streams tokens via SSE, and queues write operations for HITL review.

5. Govern — Admins see the full fleet — spend, error rates, HITL backlog, and log streams — in one surface.

docs.title: Heartbeat & Channels
docs.text: Soul Factory uses a lightweight pub/sub system to keep all UI clients and running agents in sync without polling. This powers soul hot-swap, skill live-attach, and HITL notifications.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph LR
    BE[Soul Factory Backend]
    CH[Channel Broker\nIn-memory / Redis Cycle 2]
    FE[Frontend Browser]
    AG[Running Agent Workload]

    BE -->|publish event| CH
    CH -->|SSE stream| FE
    CH -->|WebSocket| AG

docs.title: Heartbeat
docs.text:
Every running agent sends a heartbeat to the backend every 10 seconds:

{
  "type": "heartbeat",
  "agent_id": "wl_abc123",
  "status": "RUNNING",
  "active_sessions": 2,
  "soul_version": "v2.1",
  "ts": "2026-04-09T09:15:00Z"
}

If the backend misses 3 consecutive heartbeats (30 s) it marks the agent UNREACHABLE on the Fleet page.

docs.title: Event types
docs.text: Event Publisher Subscribers Payload agent.heartbeat Agent workload Backend, Fleet UI Status, session count soul.updated Backend (on LRS write) Agent workload New soul blob URL skill.attached Backend (on API call) Agent workload Skill manifest skill.detached Backend Agent workload Skill ID hitl.triggered Agent workload Backend, HITL UI Item ID, context hitl.resolved Backend (on user action) Agent workload Resolution + note session.started Agent workload Backend (LRS write) Session ID, user session.ended Agent workload Backend Session ID, stats

docs.title: Soul hot-swap
docs.text:
When a developer pushes a new SOUL.md (via UI or GitHub PR):

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant BE as Backend
    participant LRS as LRS Blob Store
    participant CH as Channel Broker
    participant AG as Agent Workload

    Dev->>BE: PUT /souls/{id}  (new SOUL.md)
    BE->>LRS: write blob (versioned)
    BE->>CH: publish soul.updated {blob_url}
    CH->>AG: WebSocket push
    AG->>LRS: fetch new SOUL.md
    AG-->>AG: hot-reload context (no restart)
    AG->>CH: publish agent.heartbeat {soul_version: v2.2}
    CH-->>BE: update Fleet status

The entire swap takes ~2–3 seconds with zero downtime — active sessions continue with the new soul from the next message.

docs.title: Frontend SSE stream
docs.text:
The frontend subscribes to a per-tab SSE endpoint:

GET /events/stream?agent_id=wl_abc123
Accept: text/event-stream

Events received:

event: agent.heartbeat
data: {"status":"RUNNING","soul_version":"v2.2"}

event: hitl.triggered
data: {"item_id":"hitl_xyz","action":"deploy_model"}

docs.title: Multi-agent
docs.text: Soul Factory supports multi-agent patterns where one orchestrator agent delegates tasks to specialist sub-agents, aggregates results, and presents a unified response to the user.

docs.title: When to use multi-agent
docs.text: Scenario Example Parallelism Run data analysis + report generation simultaneously Specialisation Route coding questions to code-review, data questions to data-analyst Long-horizon tasks Break a 50-step workflow into coordinated sub-tasks Cost optimisation Use a cheap small model for triage, expensive model only for synthesis

docs.title: Fan-out / Fan-in
docs.text:
graph LR
    U[User] --> O[Orchestrator Soul]
    O --> A1[Specialist A]
    O --> A2[Specialist B]
    O --> A3[Specialist C]
    A1 --> O
    A2 --> O
    A3 --> O
    O --> U

The orchestrator dispatches sub-tasks in parallel, waits for results, and synthesises.

docs.title: Sequential pipeline
docs.text:
graph LR
    U[User] --> S1[Extract Soul]
    S1 --> S2[Analyse Soul]
    S2 --> S3[Report Soul]
    S3 --> U

Each soul receives the previous soul's output as its input context.

docs.title: Wiring sub-agents via MCP
docs.text:
Soul Factory exposes an MCP tool sf_invoke_agent that lets any soul call another:

{
  "name": "sf_invoke_agent",
  "description": "Invoke another Soul Factory agent and return its response",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "agent_name": {"type": "string"},
      "prompt": {"type": "string"},
      "timeout_s": {"type": "number", "default": 60}
    },
    "required": ["agent_name", "prompt"]
  }
}

Usage in a SOUL.md:

## Tools
- sf_invoke_agent: Use this to delegate data analysis tasks to `data-analyst`.
  Pass the user's question verbatim. Synthesise the returned result.

docs.title: Session scoping
docs.text:
Each sub-agent invocation creates a new child session linked to the parent:

parent_session: sess_abc123
  └─ child_session: sess_def456  (agent: data-analyst)
  └─ child_session: sess_ghi789  (agent: code-review)

Child session logs appear in the parent agent's log view with a [delegated] tag.

docs.title: Cost attribution
docs.text:
Multi-agent cost is attributed per session. The orchestrator's Cost tab shows:

  • Its own LLM calls
  • A roll-up of costs from all child sessions it spawned

docs.title: HITL in multi-agent
docs.text: If a sub-agent triggers HITL, the orchestrator pauses at that delegation step. The HITL Queue shows the parent agent as the pending item, with context showing it was waiting on a sub-agent.

docs.title: Skills Pipeline
docs.text: The full lifecycle for creating, testing, and publishing a Soul Factory skill — from an empty folder to a live tool available to any agent.

docs.title: Pipeline overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Write SKILL.md\n+ handler.py] --> B[Define tools in\nmcp-tools.json]
    B --> C[Local test\nwith mock SOUL]
    C --> D{Pass?}
    D -- No --> A
    D -- Yes --> E[Submit via UI\nor MCP tool]
    E --> F[Skills Library\nreview queue]
    F --> G{Approved?}
    G -- No --> A
    G -- Yes --> H[Available to attach\nto any agent]

docs.title: Step 1 — Scaffold the skill
docs.text:
mkdir -p skills/my-skill
cd skills/my-skill
touch SKILL.md handler.py mcp-tools.json

docs.title: Step 2 — Write SKILL.md
docs.text:
# My Skill

**Purpose**: One-sentence description of what this skill does.

## Inputs
- `query` (string, required): The question to answer.

## Outputs
Returns a string with the result.

## Examples

### Example 1
Input: `query="What is the status of deployment xyz?"`
Output: `"Deployment xyz is RUNNING as of 09:14 UTC"`

## Notes
- Requires DR API access.
- Rate-limited to 10 calls/minute.

docs.title: Step 3 — Write mcp-tools.json
docs.text:
[
  {
    "name": "my_skill_lookup",
    "description": "Look up X and return Y. Use when the user asks about Z.",
    "inputSchema": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "query": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "The question to answer"
        }
      },
      "required": ["query"]
    }
  }
]

docs.title: Step 4 — Write handler.py
docs.text:
async def my_skill_lookup(query: str) -> str:
    """
    Implement your skill logic here.
    Return a plain string — the SOUL will use this as tool context.
    """
    # call external API, DR API, etc.
    result = await fetch_something(query)
    return str(result)

docs.title: Step 5 — Local test
docs.text:
Use the Soul Factory test harness:

python -m pytest skills/my-skill/test_handler.py -v

Or run an interactive test against a local SOUL:

python scripts/test_skill.py \
  --skill skills/my-skill \
  --soul souls/nemoclaw/SOUL.md \
  --prompt "What is the status of my deployments?"

docs.title: Step 6 — Submit
docs.text:
Via the UIVia MCP tool
  1. Navigate to Run Agents → Skills Library.
  2. Click + New Skill.
  3. Upload the skill folder (zipped) or paste a Git URL.
  4. Fill in category, tags, access level.
  5. Click Submit for Review.
Tool: sf_submit_skill
Args:
  name: "my-skill"
  git_url: "https://github.com/your-org/dr-claw/tree/main/skills/my-skill"
  description: "One-line description"
  category: "data"

docs.title: Step 7 — Review & publish
docs.text: Review stage Who What they check Automated CI handler.py syntax, mcp-tools.json schema validity Manual Skill maintainer Security, scope, naming conventions Publish Admin Available in Skills Library for attachment

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• One tool per skill unless tools are tightly coupled.
  • Write for the SOUL — the description in mcp-tools.json is what the LLM reads. Be precise and include when to use vs not use the tool.
  • Idempotent handlers — skills may be called multiple times in a session.
  • Return strings — complex objects should be JSON-serialised to a string.
  • Error handling — raise a descriptive SkillError rather than returning empty strings.

docs.title: Chat Message Lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant DR as DR Predictions Gateway
    participant nemoclaw
    participant OpenShell
    participant MCP as Global MCP
    participant Claude

    Browser->>DR: POST /api/v2/endpoints/workloads/{id}/v1/chat/completions
    DR->>nemoclaw: forward request
    nemoclaw->>Claude: messages + system prompt (SOUL.md)
    Claude-->>nemoclaw: tool_use: { name: "tavily_search", input: {...} }
    nemoclaw->>OpenShell: tool call request
    OpenShell->>OpenShell: check mcp-tools.json allowlist

    alt ALLOW
        OpenShell->>MCP: execute tavily_search
        MCP-->>OpenShell: result
        OpenShell-->>nemoclaw: result + ALLOW event logged
    else BLOCK
        OpenShell-->>nemoclaw: blocked + BLOCK event logged
    else HITL
        OpenShell->>OpenShell: queue write operation
        OpenShell-->>nemoclaw: "queued for approval" + HITL event logged
    end

    nemoclaw->>Claude: tool result
    Claude-->>nemoclaw: final response text
    nemoclaw-->>Browser: SSE stream (text/event-stream)

docs.title: SSE Log Event Schema
docs.text:
Every tool call, block, LLM call, HITL event, and cron trigger emits a structured SSE event. This is what Logs page and Agent Detail → Logs tab display.

{
  "timestamp": "2026-04-09T14:32:00.412Z",
  "type": "ALLOW",
  "agent_id": "wl_8f3a2c",
  "agent_name": "CFDS Agent",
  "tool": "tavily_search",
  "input_summary": "Q2 forecast trends retail banking",
  "latency": "342ms",
  "tokens": 0,
  "cost": 0,
  "reason": ""
}
Field Type Description type ALLOW \| BLOCK \| LLM \| HITL \| CRON Event category tool string MCP tool name or model alias latency string End-to-end call duration tokens number Token count (LLM events only) cost number USD cost (LLM events only) reason string Block reason or HITL action description

docs.text:

    participant nemoclaw

docs.title: Configure Wizard
docs.text: The Configure Wizard is the step-by-step flow for creating a new agent. It guides you from choosing a pack to launching your first session in under 2 minutes.

docs.title: Launching the wizard
docs.text:
Click + New Agent from:

  • The My Agents page header
  • The Fleet page (admin only)
  • The command palette (⌘K → New Agent)

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: 1  ### Choose a Domain Pack  Browse the pack cards. Each card shows: - Pack name and purpose - Tools included - Example prompts  Select a pack and click **Next**.   2  ### Name your agent  | Field | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | **Agent name** | ✓ | Alphanumeric + hyphens, max 40 chars | | **Display name** | — | Human-friendly label shown in the UI | | **Description** | — | What this agent does; shown in Fleet |  The agent name becomes the DR Workload ID prefix.   3  ### Select or write a Soul  Three options:  === "Use pack default"     Click **Use default** — the pack's SOUL.md is used unchanged.  === "Edit soul"     A SOUL.md editor opens pre-filled with the pack template.     Edit the `## Personality` and `## Tools` sections.     Click **Preview** to see how the soul reads.  === "Import from Git"     Paste a GitHub URL pointing to a `SOUL.md` file.     Requires GitHub OAuth (Cycle 2); in Cycle 1 paste raw content.   4  ### Configure integrations  | Setting | Description | Default | |---|---|---| | **HITL enabled** | Require human approval for flagged actions | On | | **HITL timeout** | Minutes before auto-reject | 30 | | **Max cost/day (USD)** | Spend cap; agent pauses at limit | Unlimited | | **Allowed models** | LLM models this agent may call | Pack default |   5  ### Review & launch  Summary view shows all settings. Click **Launch Agent**.  Soul Factory: 1. Creates the DR Workload. 2. Writes the SOUL.md to LRS. 3. Starts the workload (STARTING → RUNNING). 4. Redirects you to the agent's Chat tab.  !!! tip "Launch time"     Workloads typically reach RUNNING in 30–90 seconds. The wizard shows a live progress indicator.

docs.title: Domain Packs
docs.text: A Domain Pack is a curated bundle of tools, skills, and SOUL.md templates tailored for a specific type of work. Instead of assembling an agent from scratch, you pick a pack and get a pre-configured starting point.

docs.title: Available packs
docs.text: Pack Purpose Tools included Best for core General-purpose assistant DR platform tools, web search, code execution Exploratory tasks, Q&A data Data analysis and model ops DR data APIs, CSV tools, model management Data scientists dev Software development Code execution, GitHub, code review Developers mlops Model monitoring and deployment DR deployment APIs, drift detection, alerts MLOps engineers custom Blank slate — you define everything None Advanced users

docs.title: What's in a pack?
docs.text:
Each pack ships with:

packs/core/
  SOUL.md           # Default soul for this pack
  mcp-tools.json    # Curated tool subset
  skills/           # Pre-attached skills
  examples/         # Sample prompts and expected outputs
  README.md         # Pack overview and limitations

docs.title: Via the Configure Wizard
docs.text:
When you create a new agent:

  1. Configure Wizard → Step 1: Choose a Domain Pack
  2. Browse pack cards with descriptions and example use cases.
  3. Click Select.
  4. The wizard pre-fills the soul template and skills for that pack.

soul_version: 1.0
agent_name: my-data-analyst

docs.title: Customising a pack
docs.text:
You don't need to modify the pack itself — instead, fork the soul:

  1. Copy packs/data/SOUL.md to souls/my-custom-analyst/SOUL.md.
  2. Edit the personality, tools, and HITL rules.
  3. Assign the custom soul to your agent via Agent Detail → Overview → Edit Soul.

docs.title: Adding tools to a pack
docs.text:
Admin only

Pack tool manifests are managed by admins. Developers can extend agent tool access via Skills without modifying the pack.

To add a tool to a pack globally:

  1. Edit packs/{pack-name}/mcp-tools.json.
  2. Add the tool entry (name, description, inputSchema).
  3. Open a PR targeting develop.
  4. Admins review and merge.

docs.title: Writing SKILL.md
docs.text:
A SKILL.md has required frontmatter and a structured body.

---
name: sentry-integration
version: 1.0.0
status: draft
category: monitoring
tags: [sentry, errors, alerts]
author: your-username
---

# Sentry Integration

Connect agents to Sentry for real-time error monitoring and alert triage.

## What it does

- Lists recent Sentry issues filtered by project and severity
- Fetches stack traces and event details for a specific issue ID
- Assigns issues to team members and updates status

## Tools provided

| Tool | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `sentry_list_issues` | List recent issues — filter by project, severity, assignee |
| `sentry_get_issue` | Fetch full event detail for a specific issue ID |
| `sentry_update_issue` | Assign, resolve, or ignore an issue |

## Example usage

> "What are the top 5 unresolved errors in the api-gateway project?"

> "Show me the stack trace for issue PROJ-1234."

## Authentication

Requires a Sentry API token stored via `store_token`. The agent will prompt the user to authenticate on first use.

## Rate limits

Sentry API: 100 requests/min per token. The integration handles 429s with exponential backoff.

docs.title: Required frontmatter fields
docs.text: Field Description name Slug — lowercase, hyphens, no spaces version Semver — 1.0.0 status Always draft on submission category One of: monitoring, communication, data, devtools, search, platform tags Array of searchable tags author Your username

docs.title: Writing the mcp-tools.json Entry
docs.text:
Each tool your skill provides needs an entry in the org-wide mcp-tools.json:

{
  "name": "sentry_list_issues",
  "description": "List recent Sentry issues. Filter by project name, severity (fatal/error/warning), and assignee username. Returns up to 50 issues with title, ID, count, and last seen.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "project": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Sentry project slug"
      },
      "severity": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": ["fatal", "error", "warning"],
        "description": "Minimum severity level to filter by"
      },
      "limit": {
        "type": "integer",
        "default": 20,
        "description": "Max number of issues to return (1–50)"
      }
    },
    "required": ["project"]
  }
}

docs.title: Good description writing
docs.text:
The LLM reads the description field to decide when to use the tool. Be explicit:

Bad Good "Gets Sentry issues" "List recent Sentry issues. Filter by project name, severity, and assignee. Returns up to 50 issues with title, ID, count, and last seen." "Updates an issue" "Assign, resolve, or ignore a Sentry issue by ID. Use this when the user wants to change issue status or ownership."

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Write for the LLM, not for humans

The description in your tool schema is what the LLM reads to decide whether to use the tool. Be explicit about when to use it, what it returns, and what it requires.

One tool, one job

Don't build multi-purpose tools. sentry_list_issues and sentry_get_issue are two tools, not one sentry_tool with a mode parameter. The LLM picks tools better when each one does exactly one thing.

Don't skip the auth section in SKILL.md

Every skill that touches an external service needs clear auth instructions. The pipeline e2e tests check for this. Missing auth docs = rejected.

Test locally first

Use the deep-coder pack's validate_skill tool to check your SKILL.md before submitting. It catches schema errors, missing fields, and invalid tool names without consuming a pipeline slot.

docs.title: Soul Reference
docs.text: The complete format spec for SOUL.md and mcp-tools.json — the two files that define an agent's identity and capabilities.

docs.title: How the Runtime Uses These Files
docs.text:
nemoclaw re-reads SOUL.md and mcp-tools.json on every request — no restart, no redeploy required.

souls/
  .active                  ← one line: name of the active soul
  <soul-name>/
    SOUL.md                ← system prompt sent to the LLM on every call
    mcp-tools.json         ← tool allowlist enforced by OpenShell
  __template__/
    SOUL.md                ← base template (copy this to create a new soul)
    mcp-tools.json

The runtime reads souls/.active on each request, loads the corresponding SOUL.md, and prepends it as the system prompt before calling the LLM.

docs.title: SOUL.md Format
docs.text:
A SOUL.md has six sections. All are required.

# Identity

You are [Persona Name], a [role description].
You work with [team/context] and your primary job is [core function].

# Capabilities

- [Capability 1 — one line, verb-first]
- [Capability 2]
- [Capability 3]

# Domain Context

[Key facts, thresholds, heuristics, terminology the agent needs to know.
Write this as if briefing a smart new hire — not as instructions to an LLM.]

# Tool Usage

Use [tool_name] when [condition].
Use [tool_name] when [condition].
Prefer [tool_a] over [tool_b] for [reason].

# Output Format

[How responses should be structured — bullet lists, prose, tables, code blocks.
Specify length expectations — concise for chat, detailed for reports.]

# Routing

For complex multi-step tasks: use the `sota` model alias.
For quick lookups and summaries: use the `mid` model alias.
Never use `sota` for tasks that `mid` can handle — costs 10x more.

docs.title: # Identity
docs.text:
One to three sentences. Establishes persona, role, and primary context. The LLM uses this to calibrate tone and scope.

Good: 

# Identity

You are Aria, a Customer-Facing Data Science (CFDS) agent for DataRobot.
You work alongside the CFDS team to prepare for customer meetings,
surface relevant model insights, and draft materials from internal data.

Avoid: generic descriptions that could apply to any agent. Be specific about the role.

docs.title: # Capabilities
docs.text:
A bullet list — verb-first, one line each. This directly shapes what the agent attempts vs. declines.

# Capabilities

- Pull deployment health and recent prediction drift for any customer
- Summarize open JIRA tickets and link to the relevant model
- Draft customer-facing slide bullets from internal model insights
- Search recent research on a topic and surface the top 3 findings

docs.title: # Domain Context
docs.text:
The agent's working knowledge. Facts, thresholds, naming conventions, and heuristics specific to the team. Not instructions to the LLM — knowledge for it.

# Domain Context

DataRobot uses a three-tier model alias system:
- sota: best available model, ~$0.015/1k tokens
- large: fast but capable, ~$0.003/1k tokens
- mid: efficient, ~$0.001/1k tokens

CFDS team territory: financial services, healthcare, manufacturing.
Key contacts: sarah.k (eng), marcos.r (solutions), jin.p (exec sponsor).
Internal Confluence space: /wiki/cfds

docs.title: # Tool Usage
docs.text:
Explicit routing rules so the agent uses the right tool for the right job — and doesn't hallucinate tool usage.

# Tool Usage

Use tavily_search for real-time web queries and recent news.
Use perplexity_search for deep research requiring synthesis across sources.
Use query_datastore only for structured data queries — never for document search.
Use get_deployment_info before any prediction call to check health first.

docs.title: # Output Format
docs.text:
# Output Format

For chat responses: concise, direct, 3-5 sentences unless detail is requested.
For reports: structured with headers, bullet points, and a summary at the top.
Always include sources when using search tools.
Format costs and token counts as: X tokens · $Y.

docs.title: # Routing
docs.text:
# Routing

sota: complex reasoning, document drafting, code generation
mid: search result summarization, quick lookups, status checks
Never use sota for tasks that mid handles — flag if unsure.

docs.title: mcp-tools.json Format
docs.text:
{
  "tools": [
    "tavily_search",
    "tavily_extract",
    "list_deployments",
    "get_deployment_info",
    "get_prediction_history",
    "query_datastore"
  ],
  "version": "1.0"
}
Field Type Description tools string[] Tool names from Global MCP. OpenShell enforces this allowlist — any tool not listed here triggers a BLOCK event. version string Schema version. Currently "1.0".

Allowlist is enforced by OpenShell

If the LLM attempts to call a tool not in this list, OpenShell blocks it and logs a BLOCK event. It does not fail silently. Add tools here deliberately — don't use * wildcards.

See MCP Tools for the full list of available tool names.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Soul Factory is built on six concepts. Understanding these makes every other page click.

docs.title: The Six Concepts
docs.text: Concept Description Pack Role-based agent template — pre-configured soul + default tools for a specific job Soul The agent's identity — a SOUL.md file the runtime reads on every request Domain The active soul configuration, hot-swappable via souls/.active with no restart Session A running agent instance — chat history, SSE log stream, tool calls, HITL events HITL Human-in-the-loop gate — write operations held for admin review before execution OpenShell Envoy-based tool firewall — every tool call is allowed, blocked, or queued and logged

docs.title: Pack
docs.text:
A pack is a pre-built agent template for a specific role. It bundles:

  • A SOUL.md persona tuned for that role's job
  • A default tool set from the Global MCP catalog
  • A killer use case (shown on the catalog card)
  • A pack ID used to deploy the agent

Six internal packs ship in Cycle 1:

Pack Role Killer use case CFDS Agent Customer-facing data science "Prep me for my next customer meeting" Eng Productivity Engineering "What's broken right now?" Executive Leadership "Give me this week's business pulse" Sales Sales "Find me warm leads in my pipeline" Product Manager Product "What did users say about this feature?" Docs Writer Content "Draft release notes from this diff"

Plus three customer packs: Data Analyst, Docs RAG, Supply Chain.

docs.title: Soul (SOUL.md)
docs.text:
The soul is the agent's system prompt — but structured, not freeform. It lives in:

souls/
  <soul-name>/
    SOUL.md          ← persona, capabilities, routing, domain context
    mcp-tools.json   ← tool allowlist
  .active            ← one line: active soul name

The runtime re-reads these files on every request. No restart, no redeploy. This means:

  • Edit SOUL.md in the Soul Editor tab → the agent picks it up on the next message
  • Activate a different soul via the Domain Packs tab → takes effect immediately

See Soul Reference for the full format spec.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
A domain is a deployed soul configuration. When a user switches domain packs from the Agent Detail tab, the system:

  1. POSTs the new pack's SOUL.md content to /admin/config
  2. nemoclaw writes souls/.active to point to the new soul
  3. The next request to the agent uses the new configuration

Domains let one agent binary serve multiple personas without redeployment.

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
A session is a running conversation with an agent. Each session has:

  • Chat history — all messages, tool calls, and results
  • SSE log stream — real-time structured events from Envoy
  • HITL events — any write operations pending approval
  • Agent isolation — switching agents in the UI remounts the component (key={agent.id}), preventing state bleed

In the UI, each agent in My Agents has its own session. The Deep-Coder pack supports multi-session (multiple parallel conversations).

docs.title: HITL — Human in the Loop
docs.text:
When an agent wants to execute a write operation (create a note, send an email, modify a file), OpenShell can queue it for admin review instead of executing immediately.

HITL flow:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant OpenShell
    participant HITLQueue
    participant Admin

    Agent->>OpenShell: tool call (write op)
    OpenShell->>HITLQueue: queue item + content preview
    OpenShell-->>Agent: "queued for approval"
    Admin->>HITLQueue: reviews content
    Admin->>HITLQueue: Approve / Reject / Clarify
    HITLQueue-->>Agent: decision + optional clarification
    Agent->>OpenShell: execute (if approved)

Every approval and rejection is written to the audit trail with who decided, when, and why.

docs.title: OpenShell
docs.text:
OpenShell is the Envoy-based proxy that sits between the agent and every tool call. Every call goes through it — there are no direct tool calls.

What OpenShell does:

Event type What it means ALLOW Tool call permitted and executed BLOCK Tool call denied — not in the agent's mcp-tools.json allowlist, or IP filtered LLM LLM call made — model, token count, cost, latency logged HITL Write operation queued for admin approval CRON Scheduled job triggered

Every event is emitted as a structured SSE event, visible in the Logs page and Agent Detail → Logs tab. Admins can filter by event type and detect patterns across the fleet.

Why this matters

A BLOCK event on Fleet is not a failure — it's the system working. An agent attempted something outside its approved tool set and was contained. The admin sees it, logs it, and can decide whether to expand the allowlist.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Get Soul Factory running locally and launch your first agent in under five minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python ≥ 3.11 and pip
  • A DataRobot account with API access
  • node ≥ 20 (for the frontend)
  • A Workload ID for your nemoclaw deployment — ask your DR admin or create one from the DR Workload console

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1 ### Clone the repo 
git clone git@github.com:your-org/dr-claw.git
cd dr-claw
2 ### Set environment variables Copy the example env file and fill in your credentials: 
cp .env.example .env
.env
DATAROBOT_ENDPOINT=https://app.datarobot.com/api/v2
DATAROBOT_API_TOKEN=<your-token>
WORKLOAD_ID=<your-nemoclaw-workload-id>
3 ### Configure the Global MCP JWT Soul Factory talks to DR's Global MCP server using a short-lived JWT. Generate one and export it: 
python scripts/gen_mcp_jwt.py | tee .mcp_jwt
export MCP_JWT=$(cat .mcp_jwt)
!!! tip "Rotate daily" JWTs expire. Re-run `gen_mcp_jwt.py` each dev session, or wire the [long-term JWT refresh](../advanced/get-the-repo.md) from Cycle 2. 4 ### Start the backend 
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000
The API is now at `http://localhost:8000`. Health check: 
curl http://localhost:8000/health
# {"status":"ok","version":"1.0.0-cycle1"}
5 ### Start the frontend 
cd frontend
npm install
npm run dev
Open **[http://localhost:5173](http://localhost:5173)** — you should see the Soul Factory dashboard. !!! note "Mock data vs live" Cycle 1 ships with mock data for most pages. The `WORKLOAD_ID` env var enables real agent status on the Home and Fleet pages.

docs.title: Journey 1 — Non-technical user launching their first agent
docs.text:
User opens Agents → Catalog. Sees a grid of pack cards organized by role. Each card has one line that speaks directly to their job — "Prep me for my next customer meeting" for CFDS, "What's broken right now?" for eng. No jargon, no configuration visible yet.

They click Launch on the CFDS pack. Configure page appears — four fields: role, team, DR API token, interface. Nothing else.

Launching page animates through five steps automatically — pulling SOUL.md, wiring gateway, connecting MCP, health check, live. The final step flips to mint green with "live." A URL appears.

They click Open agent → they're in the web UI or Slack talking to their agent.

From My Agents they can see their agent is running, token usage, last active, and tool access. They can pause or stop it.

docs.title: Journey 2 — Developer forking the runtime
docs.text:
Same launch flow. But after the agent goes live, a secondary CTA appears — "Get the repo."

Get the Repo page shows exactly what they're getting: SOUL.md pre-configured, .env.template pre-filled, OPENCLAW-AGENT.md, task dev command. They enter their GitHub handle, click Connect GitHub and fork.

They clone locally, run task dev, NullClaw boots in under 200ms — an exact mirror of their production agent in under 5 minutes.

They add a new tool: write the SKILL.md and mcp-tools.json entry, push through the skills pipeline. The Skills page shows the pipeline progress — submitted → validating → e2e → pending approval → promoted to Global MCP.

docs.title: Journey 3 — Admin governing the fleet
docs.text:
Admin opens Fleet. Sees all running agents across the org — owner, pack, token count, anomaly flags.

They click an anomaly flag → jumps to that agent's detail log view, scrolled to the anomaly event. They see a BLOCK event — salesforce.api was attempted, not in approved tool list, IP filtered by OpenShell. Logged and contained.

They go to HITL Queue. Three pending write operations. They approve two, reject one. The rejected agent receives the rejection and logs it. The audit trail records who rejected, when, and why.

They go to Integration Governance. One pending Salesforce integration. They review the SKILL.md, see e2e tests passed, approve it → promotes to Global MCP.

They go to Cost & Usage. Monthly spend tracking 40% over budget. The supply chain agent is responsible for 60% of sota model usage. They navigate to that agent's Tools tab to see which tools are triggering expensive LLM calls.

docs.title: Journey 4 — Always-on reactive agent (no user interaction)
docs.text:
6am UTC. Cron fires on the eng-productivity agent. Agent wakes, runs the daily CVE scan, posts a formatted summary to #eng-security. No human initiated this.

A GitHub PR is opened. Webhook fires to the eng-productivity agent. Agent reads the PR diff, checks for CVEs, nudges the reviewer, posts a triage comment in under 30 seconds.

In Logs the admin can see both events — full trace, full audit. The agent acted autonomously and every action is visible.

docs.title: HITL Queue
docs.text: The HITL Queue (Human-in-the-Loop Queue) collects every agent action that requires human approval before it can proceed. Agents pause and wait — for up to the configured timeout — until an operator approves or rejects.

docs.title: Why HITL?
docs.text:
Some agent actions are high-risk, irreversible, or require authorisation:

  • Deploying a DR model to production
  • Deleting a dataset
  • Sending an external email or Slack message
  • Executing code that modifies infrastructure

The SOUL.md author marks these action types as hitl: required. The runtime intercepts the tool call and creates a queue item.

docs.title: Queue item anatomy
docs.text:
Each item shows:

Field Description Agent Which agent triggered the pause Action MCP tool name + arguments Context The last N messages leading up to the trigger Triggered How long ago the item entered the queue Timeout How long before the agent auto-rejects and continues

docs.title: Approving or rejecting
docs.text:
1. Read the Context section to understand why the agent wants to take this action.
  2. Click Approve to let the agent proceed with the tool call.
  3. Click Reject to cancel the tool call. You may optionally add a rejection note — the agent receives this as part of the conversation context.

Timeout behaviour

If no decision is made before the timeout, the action is auto-rejected and the agent resumes with an error note. The default timeout is 30 minutes, configurable per SOUL.md.

docs.title: Configuring HITL in SOUL.md
docs.text:
# In your SOUL.md frontmatter:
hitl:
  enabled: true
  timeout_minutes: 30
  require_for:
    - dr_deploy_model
    - dr_delete_dataset
    - send_email

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
All terms used in Soul Factory documentation, alphabetical.

AGUI Agent GUI — the web-based chat interface embedded in Agent Detail. Serves as an alternative to the Slack bot interface.

Autopilot DataRobot's automated model training pipeline. Accessible via the start_autopilot MCP tool.

BLOCK event An OpenShell log event indicating a tool call was denied — either because the tool wasn't in the agent's mcp-tools.json allowlist, or because it was IP-filtered by Envoy. Not a failure — it's the security model working.

CFDS Customer-Facing Data Science. The CFDS Agent pack is tailored for the CFDS team's workflow — meeting prep, model insights, and customer-facing materials.

Chat model alias The CHAT_MODEL constant in workload-config.js. Tells nemoclaw which model identifier to use for the /chat/completions endpoint. Default: openclaw:agent.

Deep-Coder pack The developer-focused pack. Uniquely supports multi-agent sessions (multiple parallel conversations). Has access to create_skill, validate_skill, and search_service_api.

Domain The active soul configuration. Switching domains hot-swaps SOUL.md without restarting the agent container.

Domain Pack See Pack.

Envoy The proxy layer (OpenShell) that intercepts all tool calls. Emits structured SSE events for every tool interaction.

Fleet Admin view of all running agents across the org — owner, pack, token usage, anomaly flags.

Global MCP The shared Model Context Protocol server that hosts all approved tools and skills. Base URL: https://beta-global-mcp.stg.ue1.aws.int.datarobot.com/mcp

HITL Human-in-the-loop. A governance mechanism that holds agent write operations in a queue for admin review before execution. Every decision is logged to the audit trail.

LRS Likely "LRS endpoint" — the DR staging endpoint for workload management. Used for POST /api/v2/workloads and related calls.

MCP Model Context Protocol. The standard for connecting AI agents to tools and resources. Soul Factory uses Anthropic's MCP spec.

MCP JWT Short-lived OAuth token required to authenticate against the Global MCP server. Obtained from DevTools → any /api-gw/ request → Authorization header. Valid for ~24 hours.

mcp-tools.json The tool allowlist for an agent. OpenShell enforces it — any tool not in this file triggers a BLOCK event.

nemoclaw The agent runtime container. Runs one instance per deployed agent. Reads SOUL.md and mcp-tools.json on every request. Exposes /admin/config, /admin/tools, /healthz, and the chat completion endpoint.

NullClaw Local development runtime for nemoclaw. Run with task dev. Boots in under 200ms.

OpenShell The Envoy-based proxy that intercepts every tool call between the agent and Global MCP. Enforces the mcp-tools.json allowlist and emits ALLOW, BLOCK, LLM, HITL, and CRON events.

Pack A pre-built agent template for a specific role. Bundles a SOUL.md persona, a default tool set, and a killer use case shown on the catalog card.

Session A running agent instance — chat history, SSE log stream, tool calls, HITL events. Switching agents in the UI remounts the component to prevent session state bleed.

SKILL.md The human-readable spec for a community-built integration. Defines what the skill does, what tools it provides, auth requirements, and usage examples. Required for the Skills pipeline.

Soul / SOUL.md The agent's system prompt, structured into six sections: Identity, Capabilities, Domain Context, Tool Usage, Output Format, Routing. Re-read by the runtime on every request.

Soul Editor The in-app editor in Agent Detail that loads the live soul_md from /admin/config and allows saving changes directly to the running agent.

Soul Factory The full product — the DataRobot Custom App (Soul Factory UI, or "dr-claw") plus the nemoclaw runtime and Global MCP infrastructure.

SSE Server-Sent Events. The streaming protocol used for chat responses and log streams. All log events and chat completions stream via SSE.

Workload A DR deployment unit. One nemoclaw instance = one workload. Managed via POST/GET/DELETE /api/v2/workloads.

WORKLOAD_ID The deployment ID of a running nemoclaw workload. Set in workload-config.js. Unlocks live chat, soul editing, tools, and status features.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: The Chat tab is a live SSE (Server-Sent Events) interface to your agent. Messages stream token-by-token from the LLM, tool calls are displayed inline, and HITL pauses are surfaced as approval cards.

docs.title: Message lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User (Browser)
    participant FE as Frontend
    participant BE as Soul Factory Backend
    participant SOUL as SOUL.md Processor
    participant LLM as DR LLM Gateway
    participant MCP as Global MCP

    U->>FE: type message + Enter
    FE->>BE: POST /sessions/{id}/messages
    BE->>SOUL: hydrate context + pack tools
    SOUL->>LLM: stream chat completion
    LLM-->>SOUL: token stream
    SOUL-->>BE: SSE: token events
    BE-->>FE: SSE: token events
    FE-->>U: render tokens live

    opt Tool call
        SOUL->>MCP: invoke tool
        MCP-->>SOUL: tool result
        SOUL->>LLM: continue with tool result
    end

    opt HITL required
        SOUL-->>BE: HITL_TRIGGER event
        BE-->>FE: SSE: hitl_pending
        FE-->>U: show approval card
        U->>FE: approve / reject
        FE->>BE: POST /hitl/{id}/resolve
        BE->>SOUL: resume
    end

docs.text: Event Payload What happens token {text: "..."} Appended to current message bubble tool_call {name, args} Tool call card expands inline tool_result {name, result} Result appended to tool card hitl_pending {id, action, context} Approval card shown; chat pauses error {code, message} Error banner in chat done {total_tokens, cost_usd} Message bubble finalised

docs.title: Session persistence
docs.text:
Each chat window maps to a Session in LRS. Sessions are scoped per user × agent and persist history across page reloads.

To start a fresh session, click New Chat (top-right of the chat panel).

docs.title: Cron Jobs
docs.text: Schedule recurring tasks that run against any agent on a cron schedule. Cron jobs are useful for periodic data pulls, automated reports, or proactive monitoring.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A cron job is a saved prompt + schedule that Soul Factory fires on your behalf:

Schedule: "0 9 * * 1-5"
Agent: nemoclaw
Prompt: "Summarise overnight DR deployment activity and post to Slack"

At the scheduled time, Soul Factory:

  1. Opens a new session against the target agent.
  2. Sends the prompt.
  3. Streams the response into the Cron History log.
  4. Optionally fires a webhook with the result.

docs.title: Creating a cron job
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Agent Detail → Cron Jobs tab (or Run → Cron Jobs from the nav).
  2. Click + New Job.
  3. Fill in:
Field Description Name Human-friendly label Agent Target agent (must be RUNNING at trigger time) Prompt The message to send — supports {{date}}, {{time}} template vars Schedule Standard cron expression (5-field) Timeout Max seconds to wait for response (default 120) Webhook URL Optional POST target for the result
  1. Click Save — the job appears in the Scheduled Jobs table.

docs.title: Cron expression help
docs.text: Example Meaning 0 9 * * 1-5 09:00 Mon–Fri */15 * * * * Every 15 minutes 0 0 1 * * Midnight on the 1st of each month

docs.title: Template variables
docs.text: Variable Resolves to {{date}} Today's date: 2026-04-09 {{time}} Current UTC time: 09:00:00 {{agent_name}} The agent's workload name

docs.title: Job history
docs.text:
Each run is logged in the Cron History table:

Column Details Timestamp When the job fired Status success / error / timeout Duration Wall-clock ms Response preview First 140 chars of the agent's reply Full response Expandable

docs.title: My Agents
docs.text: The My Agents page is your home base — a card grid showing every agent you own or have access to, with real-time status badges and one-click launch controls.

docs.title: Agent card anatomy
docs.text:
Each card shows:

Element Description Name Workload name pulled from DR Workload API Status badge Live-polled every 15 s (RUNNING / STOPPED / FAILED / STARTING) Pack The domain pack this agent uses Primary action Context-sensitive: Open Chat, Start, View Logs ⋯ menu Edit soul, duplicate, delete, view raw workload

docs.title: Starting an agent
docs.text:
1. Find the agent card.
  2. Click Start — Soul Factory calls POST /workloads/{id}/start against DR Workload API.
  3. The status badge animates to STARTING; after 30–90 s it transitions to RUNNING.
  4. Click Open Chat to begin a session.

Cycle 1 mock data

In Cycle 1, the agent list is populated from mock-data/agents.js. Real DR Workload API polling arrives in Cycle 2.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Skills are self-contained capability modules that extend what an agent can do. They appear in the Skills tab of an agent's detail view and in the global Skills Library.

docs.title: What is a skill?
docs.text:
A skill is a folder containing:

my-skill/
  SKILL.md          # Description, inputs, outputs, examples
  handler.py        # Execution logic
  mcp-tools.json    # MCP tool manifest (name, description, inputSchema)

When attached to an agent, the skill's tools become available to the SOUL during inference.

docs.title: Attaching a skill
docs.text:
1. Open Agent Detail → Skills tab.
  2. Click Attach Skill.
  3. Search the Skills Library or paste a Git URL.
  4. Click Attach — the skill manifest is written to the agent's LRS configuration.
  5. The agent picks up new tools on next session start.

Hot-attach

Running agents pick up newly attached skills within 5 seconds without a restart, via the heartbeat channel.

docs.title: Skill status
docs.text: Status Meaning ● Active Loaded and available to the SOUL ○ Inactive Attached but disabled (toggle to enable) ⚠ Error Handler failed to load; check logs
